name: simple previous verse

name: variant wording

name: next verse
text: Paul says in Romans 8:1 that there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. The next verse explains why.

name: same chapter, explicit verse number
text: John 3 introduces the conversation with Nicodemus. In verse 16, the language broadens from the conversation itself to God’s love for the world.

name: later in the chapter
text: Jesus first speaks privately with Nicodemus in John 3. Later in the chapter, the focus returns to John the Baptist and his testimony about Jesus.

name: preceding chapter

name: first half of next verse
text: In 1 Corinthians 13:1 Paul describes speech without love as empty noise. The first half of the next verse shifts from speech to prophecy, knowledge, and faith.

name: multiple fuzzy references in one paragraph
text: John 6:35 begins with Jesus’ declaration, “I am the bread of life.” In the previous verse, the crowd asks him to give them this bread always. A few verses later, Jesus begins to explain that no one can come to him unless the Father draws that person. Later in the chapter, the discussion becomes increasingly difficult for his hearers.

name: competing recent anchors
text: John 3:16 is often read alongside Numbers 21:8–9 because Jesus has just compared his coming death to the bronze serpent. In the next verse, the emphasis turns from God’s love to God’s purpose in sending the Son.

name: not a Bible reference

name: ambiguous “chapter 6”
text: John has already introduced the signs theme and Jesus’ growing conflict with his opponents. In chapter 6, the feeding of the crowd leads into the bread-of-life discourse.

name: ambiguous “chapter 6” with weak context
text: The discussion of bread becomes much more important in chapter 6.

name: “those verses”
text: Romans 8:18–23 describes creation as groaning while it waits for liberation. Those verses frame suffering as part of a larger hope rather than as an isolated problem.

name: “the passage above”
text: In Ephesians 2:11–22 Paul describes Gentiles being brought near and joined into one new humanity. The passage above depends heavily on spatial imagery: far away, near, dividing wall, access, household, foundation, temple.

name: “earlier in the chapter”
text: In Romans 8:28 Paul says that all things work together for good for those who love God. Earlier in the chapter, however, he has already framed Christian experience in terms of weakness, suffering, and groaning.

name: long paragraph with mixed explicit and fuzzy references
text: The bread-of-life discourse develops over a long stretch of John 6. Jesus identifies himself as the bread of life in verse 35, but that statement does not appear out of nowhere. In the previous verse the crowd has asked him to give them this bread always. A little later, Jesus explains that those who come to him will not be cast out, and several verses after that he returns to the image of bread from heaven. Near the end of the chapter, many disciples complain that the teaching is difficult, and in the following verses some of them turn back and stop following him.

name: long paragraph with a non-Bible “previous chapter”
text: The author has spent most of this chapter discussing how nineteenth-century commentators understood Paul’s rhetoric. Romans 7:14–25 appears several times as an example. The previous chapter of this book focused instead on patristic interpretation, especially Augustine. In the next verse, Paul shifts back to the first person.

name: contextual book inheritance across sentences

Chapter 6 begins with rejection at Nazareth and then moves through the mission of the Twelve, the death of John the Baptist, and the feeding miracle. Near the end of the chapter, Jesus walks on the sea.
